title: Emergent Sparsity: How Many Effective Variables Survive Coarse-Graining in AlphaEarth Embeddings?
abstract: AlphaEarth encodes each 10 m land pixel as a 64-component vector intended to support diverse global mapping tasks. Yet many scientific applications work at coarser spatial supports, for which fewer than 64 effective variables may suffice. We ask whether these vectors can be reorganized into ranked global nonlinear coordinates, how many suffice at a chosen reconstruction accuracy, and whether that number decreases with spatial scale. We thus describe effective dimension as a two-control surface over tolerance and spatial scale, rather than one intrinsic number. At each scale, a $β$-VAE scan with a common architecture produces a rank--distortion envelope, giving the smallest retained count achieved within the scanned family at each reconstruction tolerance. At 3% validation tolerance, this number falls from 24 to 7 when the scale is increased from 10 m to 78.9 km, whereas the corresponding PCA rank falls only from 46 to 38. Repeating the analysis on unit-norm targets preserves this trend.
summary: This paper analyzes the effective dimensionality of global Earth embeddings by testing how many variables are needed to reconstruct the data when averaging over larger spatial scales. Using $\beta$-VAEs, the authors find that the required number of variables drops significantly as the scale increases, demonstrating that effective dimension depends on both the desired accuracy and the spatial averaging scale.
main_problem: To determine how the effective number of variables required to represent global Earth observations decreases when the spatial support is coarse-grained, and how this dependence relates to reconstruction accuracy.
main_result: The effective dimension is a two-control surface dependent on both reconstruction tolerance and spatial scale, showing a significant reduction in required variables (e.g., from 24 to 7) when moving from 10 m to 78.9 km scale.
method: The study uses $\beta$-Variational Autoencoders ($\beta$-VAEs) to learn nonlinear coordinates and compares the resulting effective dimension against Principal Component Analysis (PCA) ranks across varying spatial scales and reconstruction tolerances.
model_or_system: The system uses AlphaEarth embeddings, which encode global land pixel data into 64-component vectors. The analysis investigates the intrinsic dimensionality of this embedding field across scales ranging from 10 m to 78.9 km.
key_observables: Effective Dimension ($	ext{deff}$), Reconstruction Tolerance ($\epsilon$), Spatial Scale ($\ell$), Rank-Distortion Curves, and coordinate association coefficients ($\phi_K$).
important_parameters: Reconstruction tolerance (e.g., 3%), Spatial scale ($\ell$) (e.g., 10 m to 78.9 km), and the VAE regularization parameter ($ eta$).
main_assumptions: The effective dimension estimate is an empirical upper bound, and the analysis relies on fitting functional forms (e.g., power laws) to the observed scale dependence.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate validation scale–tolerance contours comparing VAE and PCA performance, and show the relationship between retained coordinates and environmental variables like temperature and precipitation.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem by defining effective dimension as a surface $	ext{deff}(\epsilon, \ell)$. It details the VAE/PCA methodology, presents the core finding of scale-dependent dimension reduction, and concludes by deriving analytical approximations for this dependence.
why_interesting: While the application is geophysical, the mathematical framework—determining the effective degrees of freedom of a high-dimensional embedding field under coarse-graining—is analogous to concepts in renormalization group theory or dimensionality reduction in complex many-body systems.
